title: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.
lead: An agency abandons its passive-restraint standard after manufacturers choose detachable belts, and the insurers ask why that justified abandoning every available alternative.

actors.name: NHTSA
actors.role: Transportation agency responsible for motor-vehicle safety standards.

actors.name: State Farm and National Association of Independent Insurers
actors.role: Insurers seeking review of the rescission.

actors.name: Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association and Department of Transportation
actors.role: Parties defending the rescission in the Supreme Court.

proceedings: NHTSA rescinded the passive-restraint requirement after notice, comments, and hearings.
The D.C. Circuit set the rescission aside and ordered administrative reconsideration.
The Supreme Court vacated the appellate judgment and remanded for return to NHTSA under the correct review standard.
limits: The figures describe the historical record. The decision required reasoned reconsideration, not airbags in every car. Later textbook developments and editorial critiques are distinct from the 1983 holding.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A safety program moves beyond manually fastened belts
sections.cue: What problem did passive restraints address?
paragraphs: The National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act instructed the Secretary of Transportation to establish practicable, objective standards meeting motor-vehicle safety needs. Available safety data, reasonableness, practicability, and contribution to statutory purposes mattered. Congress expressly subjected establishment, amendment, and revocation of standards to APA review. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, or NHTSA, exercised the Secretary’s delegated authority.

Standard 208 evolved because installing manual seatbelts did not ensure that occupants used them. Passive restraints would operate without a new affirmative choice each trip. Airbags inflate in a crash; automatic belts deploy as occupants enter or operate the car. Congress prohibited reliance on ignition interlocks, which kept a car from operating unless belts were connected, and on the specified continuous warning buzzer. Whether that public resistance also discredited other restraint designs later became contested.

The 1977 Modified Standard 208 phased in passive restraints while allowing manufacturers to choose airbags or automatic belts. NHTSA expected roughly sixty percent airbags and forty percent belts. By 1981 manufacturers instead planned automatic belts for about ninety-nine percent of new cars, chiefly detachable belts that occupants could leave disconnected. The agency still accepted airbags’ effectiveness and belts’ protection when worn. The emerging issue was whether the chosen designs would increase actual use enough to justify their cost.

sections.title: NHTSA withdraws the requirement and insurers challenge its reasons
sections.cue: What did the agency decide, and why did the first reviewing court disagree?
paragraphs: After notice, written comments, and public hearings, NHTSA rescinded the passive-restraint requirement in 1981. It forecast little increased use from detachable belts, approximately one billion dollars in compliance costs, and adverse consumer reaction to expensive equipment yielding negligible benefits. It did not discuss an airbags-only standard. It grouped continuous, nondetachable belts with other devices that compelled use rather than analyzing their different operation.

State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Company and the National Association of Independent Insurers petitioned for review in the D.C. Circuit. That court found defects in the treatment of detachable belts, continuous belts, and airbags. It also inferred from congressional activity a growing commitment to passive restraints requiring increasingly strong reasons to reverse course. It directed administrative reconsideration and entered later implementation orders.

The Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association and parties in companion petitions, including the Department of Transportation, defended rescission in the Supreme Court. Justice White’s opinion agreed that NHTSA’s action could not stand, but rejected parts of the D.C. Circuit’s method. That distinction mattered to the eventual vacatur and remand.

sections.title: The Court requires an explanation for changing the existing judgment
sections.cue: Why is rescission review different from simply asking whether regulation should begin?
paragraphs: The agency urged the exceptionally narrow scrutiny associated with refusing to initiate regulation. The Court instead applied ordinary arbitrary-and-capricious review under APA § 706(2)(A). The Safety Act treated revocation like establishment and amendment, and rescission abandoned an existing regulatory judgment. An agency may change policy, but must explain why.

A court asks whether the agency examined relevant material and connected its findings to its choice. Unauthorized considerations, failure to consider an important aspect, contradiction of the record, or an explanation too implausible to reflect expertise or reasonable judgment can establish arbitrariness. Courts may follow an imperfect but discernible explanation; they may neither supply missing reasons nor substitute their preferred policy. This review of compliance with a statutory mandate differs from the minimal constitutional rationality review applied to economic legislation.

The Court also rejected the D.C. Circuit’s heightened standard. Congress’s interlock prohibition, failure to veto the 1977 rule, and unenacted proposals did not establish a different APA standard. Their meaning was uncertain, and even approval of an earlier interpretation would not necessarily control later discretion without incorporation into law. Nor did the Court hold that uncertainty could never justify rescission. A reasonable agency inference can reach beyond conclusive data, provided the explanation addresses the evidence and ordinarily explains why more information was not sought.

sections.title: Airbags remain an unexplained alternative
sections.cue: Why could counsel and Vermont Yankee not answer the omission?
paragraphs: NHTSA’s worry about detachable belts did not discredit airbags. Airbags were already an accepted, effective, cost-beneficial means of satisfying this standard. The agency needed to explain why the manufacturers’ preference justified ending the obligation altogether rather than considering an airbags requirement. Congress had authorized safety regulation partly because manufacturers had not made all needed improvements voluntarily.

Counsel suggested small-car difficulties, implementation concerns, and public resistance, but NHTSA had not actually supplied those reasons for rejecting an option it never considered. Under Chenery, post hoc litigation rationales could not repair the decision. The Court left open whether an airbags-only rule would require further notice, and recognized temporary suspension as a possible way to permit additional study.

The manufacturers invoked Vermont Yankee’s restriction on judicially invented procedures. White imposed no new hearing mechanism and no duty to discuss every imaginable alternative. Requiring analysis of an established compliance option directly implicated by withdrawal was substantive review of the reasons already required. All nine Justices agreed on the airbag defect.

sections.title: The majority questions belt assumptions; four Justices would defer further
sections.cue: Where did the Court divide over the agency’s analysis?
paragraphs: A five-Justice majority also found the automatic-belt discussion inadequate. NHTSA could question whether studies of voluntarily purchased cars, often with interlocks, predicted behavior under a universal belt requirement without interlocks. But those limits did not answer inertia: once reconnected, an automatic belt keeps working without another decision on each trip. That could increase use among occasional users, and the agency had not addressed it. The Court did not calculate the increase itself.

Costs and consumer resistance depended in turn on the disputed estimate of minimal benefit. Revisiting expected protection required revisiting that assessment. Safety remained the statute’s principal objective, though costs and practicability were relevant. Continuous belts also deserved separate treatment. NHTSA previously accepted spool-release designs as providing emergency escape, and continuous belts did not disable operation like interlocks. It could change its view, but had not explained why those differences ceased to matter.

Justice Rehnquist, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justices Powell and O’Connor, agreed with the standard, rejection of heightened congressional-history review, and airbag analysis. He expressly accepted the need to explain abandonment of previously approved airbag and continuous-spool options. His disagreement concerned detachable belts. He thought the agency reasonably declined to extrapolate from voluntary purchases involving interlocks, acknowledged some increased use, and found that increase too small to justify costs. The explanation could be clearer, but he saw a rational connection.

Rehnquist added that a new presidential administration could legitimately reassess costs, uncertainty, public resistance, and priorities. His separate opinion did not authorize disregarding Congress’s standards or refusing to enforce an unwanted statute. The majority did not treat an election alone as the missing explanation.

sections.title: The agency receives another opportunity to decide
sections.cue: What did the remand require, and what belongs to later commentary?
paragraphs: On June 24, 1983, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit’s judgment and directed a remand to NHTSA for further consideration. The agency could retain, revise, or reconsider the standard through adequate reasoning; the Court did not itself mandate airbags. It found sufficient justification for temporary suspension during reconsideration without resolving the parties’ competing descriptions of the appellate implementation order.

The eight assigned editorial notes extend the discussion beyond this holding. The first two consider electoral ideology and Secretary Coleman’s 1976 emphasis on choice, markets, costs, and equity. Those are editorial questions and an earlier agency policy, not explanations the Court accepted here. The third reports the 1984 renewed passive-protection rule, conditioned on withdrawal if qualifying belt-use laws covered two-thirds of the population before April 1, 1989; the condition never occurred. It also reports a distinct 1986 D.C. Circuit decision finding the withdrawal challenge unripe and upholding the remaining alternatives analysis.

The fourth note attributes to Mashaw and Harfst the critique that demands for documented rationality can favor established technology and delay regulation, comparing rules, recalls, and guidance. The fifth contrasts NRDC v. EPA’s reasoned prediction of future diesel trap-oxidizer development, with methodology, remaining steps, and timing rather than solved engineering demanded. The sixth illustrates authorizing statutes’ health, harassment, and cost requirements: omitted statutory considerations differ from invented court procedures.

The seventh examines remand without vacatur, defect severity, disruption, delay, and disputes over that remedy’s legality. It does not alter State Farm’s actual disposition. The eighth discusses Ohio v. EPA’s 2024 stay analysis, Barrett’s dissent, and a separate writing in Department of Commerce v. New York. Those later proceedings and critiques retain their separate source limits. Neither these notes nor the historic usage figures certify current safety statistics, Standard 208, or present citator treatment.
